The Star-nosed mole Condylura cristata occupies a unique niche among insectivorous mammals, inhabiting the saturated soils and wetland margins of eastern North America. At the time of parturition, the altricial neonate emerges weighing a mere 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams], a minute body mass that reflects the abbreviated in utero development typical of this species. This minimal starting investment is counterbalanced by an intense period of maternal care; during gestation, which lasts approximately 40 days [tg = approximately 40 days] under a core body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], the gestating embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis. The newborn, or pup, is entirely dependent on its mother for thermoregulation and nutrition. The wet weight at birth is among the smallest recorded for any talpid, highlighting the trade-off between producing a large litter and the constraints imposed by the high metabolic demands of the mole's fossorial lifestyle.

The suckling juvenile phase proceeds rapidly, driven by the energetic demands of the milk-dependent offspring. Weaning occurs at 24 days from birth [tx = 24 days from birth], a stage marked by the suckling end and the onset of nutritional independence, with the young attaining a wet weight at weaning of 30 grams [Wwx = 30 grams] at the same thermoneutral body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This tripling of birth mass over less than four weeks underscores the efficiency of the milk transfer. Following nutritional emancipation, the weaned juvenile embarks on an accelerated somatic growth trajectory, foraging independently for aquatic invertebrates and earthworms in the soft muck of the marsh. The pre-weaning pup and the early post-weaning juvenile are particularly vulnerable to predation, but the rapid acquisition of body mass helps mitigate this risk.

Sexual maturation in this species is a protracted process relative to the short weaning period. Time since birth at puberty is reached at 304 days [tp = 304 days] when core body temperature is maintained at 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], indicating that young moles do not become reproductively active until nearly a full year after birth. This delay in gonad maturation and first ovulation contrasts with the fast early growth, reflecting a life-history strategy where energy is allocated toward building a robust adult body size rather than early breeding. The pubertal onset occurs after the young mole has established its own tunnel system and secured a reliable territory. The post-pubertal adult then attains the full physiological capacity for reproduction, though actual first copulation may be deferred further by environmental conditions such as seasonal flooding or prey abundance.

In terms of adult body size, the ultimate wet weight achieved by a fully grown, reproductively viable organism is approximately 55.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 55.3 grams], a figure representing the maximum recorded body mass in adults. This adult body mass is consistent with the species' high metabolic rate, which is necessary to sustain activity in cold waterlogged soils. While the range of typical adult masses varies, with some individuals reported at 35 to 75 grams, the asymptotic mass of 55.3 grams represents a stable endpoint of somatic growth. The breeding adult mammal, particularly the gravid female, carries a substantial reproductive burden, as the combined mass of a litter of four pups places considerable energetic pressure on the lactating female during the short 40-day gestation and the subsequent three-week nursing period.

Reproductive output is constrained by the harsh seasonal environment, with females producing a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] containing an average of 4.4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4.4 pups per litter]. This annual reproductive output, while modest in frequency, results in a high reproductive rate given the small neonatal mass. Maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at approximately 2.5 years [am = approximately 2.5 years] under a core body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], a relatively short longevity that is typical of small, metabolically active mammals living in high-mortality environments. The consequence of this compressed lifespan is that a female mole has only one or two breeding seasons to replace herself, placing a premium upon the successful weaning of a single annual litter.
